stories.headline: Rockies Unveil Todd Helton Statue Outside Coors Field
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies unveiled a bronze statue of Hall of Famer Todd Helton on Saturday at 20th and Blake outside Coors Field, depicting the first baseman catching the final out that sent the club to its only World Series appearance in 2007. The 17-foot tall, 1,000-pound monument was designed by renowned Loveland sculptors George and Mark Lundeen, and was revealed by Helton's youngest daughter, Gentry Grace, about three hours before first pitch against the Seattle Mariners.

Helton, enshrined in Cooperstown in 2024 after six years on the ballot, was visibly emotional at the ceremony, reflecting on how his late father Jerry Helton — a former Twins minor-league catcher — shaped him into the player Colorado came to love. Purple and white confetti rained on Helton and his family as he described the statue as 'the ultimate honor.'

The statue completes a triumvirate of bronze figures guarding Coors Field's main entrance, joining the Larry Walker statue revealed in August and 'The Player' statue that has stood outside the stadium since its 1995 opening. Helton's monument captures the iconic freeze-frame photographed by Denver Post photographer John Leyba, showing Helton stretching to secure the throw from Troy Tulowitzki on a check-swing by Arizona's Eric Byrnes.

stories.headline: Broncos Prepare for Home Opener Against Jacksonville After Week 1 Blowout Loss
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos host the Jacksonville Jaguars Sunday at Empower Field at Mile High in their 2026 home opener, looking to rebound after a blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1. Head coach Sean Payton acknowledged widespread failures from the opener, saying 'there was dirt on a ton of people's hands, starting with me,' while noting the quick turnaround and the challenge of facing a Jacksonville team that thumped Denver in December of last year.

Key concerns heading into the matchup include quarterback Bo Nix's decision-making under pressure, with Nix missing several opportunities to connect with new receiver Jaylen Waddle despite the wideout being open multiple times. Offensive coordinator Davis Webb's play-calling debut was scrutinized, with analysts pointing to a lack of commitment to the run game and poor play sequencing on first and second downs.

The game carries added significance as a measuring-stick moment for the franchise, with Denver Post columnist Troy Renck raising questions about whether the Broncos are developing a toughness problem similar to those that plagued the Nuggets and Avalanche in recent playoff runs. Payton and the coaching staff have emphasized correcting fundamentals in a short week of preparation.

stories.headline: Avalanche Open Training Camp With Eye on Depth Around Star Core
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche opened training camp this week with their first preseason game against the Utah Mammoth scheduled for Sunday, coming off a 55-16-11 regular season and a trip to the Western Conference Finals. The roster around established stars Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar and Devon Toews has seen significant turnover, with newcomers Jaden Schwartz, Fedor Svechkov, Zachary L'Heureux and Brett Kulak projected into meaningful lineup spots.

Coach Jared Bednar is focused on identifying which supporting players can elevate an already-strong team when the stakes are highest in the playoffs. Defenseman Sam Malinski, coming off a breakout 40-point season, is competing for an expanded role alongside the team's top defensive pair.

At the rookie level, Colorado went 1-0-1 at the Rookie Faceoff, defeating Anaheim 7-2 before losing to Vegas in a shootout, with defenseman Alex Gagne recording a Gordie Howe hat trick against the Ducks. The Avalanche's relatively thin prospect pipeline puts additional emphasis on internal competition to fill depth roles before the regular season begins.

stories.headline: FEMA Denies Individual Assistance and Hazard Mitigation Funding for Colorado Wildfire Victims
stories.summary:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency has denied Colorado's requests for Individual Assistance and Hazard Mitigation Grant Program funding for communities affected by the Aspen Acres wildfire, which burned more than 100,000 acres and destroyed hundreds of homes in southern Colorado. The denial was announced by Gov. Jared Polis's office late Friday, and means residents in Pueblo and Custer counties will not receive federal help with temporary housing, home repairs, crisis counseling, disaster unemployment assistance or legal services.

The Hazard Mitigation Grant Program, which would have funded flood prevention, stormwater upgrades and wildfire mitigation efforts, was also denied. The state retains access to federal public assistance funding for debris removal and public infrastructure repairs in Custer, Dolores, Ouray and Pueblo counties, approved earlier this month. Colorado has 30 days to appeal the decision if it chooses.

Gov. Polis expressed disappointment, while U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper called on the Trump administration to reverse course, saying the requests 'are not made frivolously.' The denial follows a pattern of the administration rejecting disaster aid requests from Colorado, including for the Elk and Lee fires and western Colorado flooding in 2025. Critics have accused the administration of politicizing federal disaster relief.

stories.headline: Denver Voters Face Xcel Franchise Vote in November — But Will Pay 3% Fee Either Way
stories.summary:
Denver voters will decide in November whether to approve a new 20-year franchise agreement with Xcel Energy, but a little-noticed provision means they will continue paying a 3% franchise fee on their electric and gas bills regardless of the outcome. Page 22 of the existing agreement, which expires Dec. 31, requires Xcel to keep paying Denver an amount equal to the franchise fee as long as the utility uses city rights-of-way, a cost that is passed directly to ratepayers.

Denver and Xcel officials maintain the 3% charge — in place since 1947 — will continue after the agreement expires, generating roughly $30 million annually for the city. However, former Colorado Public Utilities Commission chairman Jeff Ackermann disputes this interpretation, arguing Xcel will have no legal authority to collect the fee on January 1 if voters reject the deal.

The proposed 20-year agreement is making its second attempt to reach the ballot after Denver City Council voted 7-6 against placing the original measure before voters last year. Faith-based nonprofit Together Colorado, which has more than 200 congregations, has organized against the long-term deal, while Denver officials argue the agreement provides benefits beyond the franchise fee revenue.

stories.headline: Medicaid Spending Could Consume Colorado's Entire General Fund Within Two Decades, Budget Chief Warns
stories.summary:
Colorado's state budget director Mark Ferrandino warned lawmakers last week that Medicaid spending, if left unchecked, could consume the entire state general fund within two decades. Ferrandino delivered the projections to the Commission on Medicaid, an interim legislative committee established this spring to address what he called a 'bona fide crisis,' noting the state could overspend its current-year Medicaid budget by $443 million and potentially by nearly $1 billion next year.

Ferrandino attributed the surge primarily to increased utilization among existing enrollees rather than enrollment growth — a paradox identified by a Common Sense Institute analysis showing the number of Colorado Medicaid enrollees dropped by more than 500,000 between 2023 and 2025 even as spending jumped 15%, or $2 billion. The state has enacted 182 health-care bills since 2019 adding $858 million annually to its Medicaid costs, including expanded services in acute care, pharmacy and behavioral health.

Medicaid already represents the largest single item in Colorado's operating budget, consuming more than a third of it and growing at nearly double the rate of state revenue increases since 2021. Lawmakers on the commission will face the findings when the legislature reconvenes in January, tasked with finding ways to rein in costs without gutting coverage for low-income and disabled residents.

stories.headline: Denver DA Will Not Charge Officer Who Shot and Killed Man Following Knife Confrontation
stories.summary:
Denver District Attorney John Walsh announced Friday that no criminal charges will be filed against Denver Police Officer Sullivan Egbert, who shot and killed 26-year-old Wilson Guerra-Bravo on July 5 after Guerra-Bravo allegedly lunged at the officer with a knife. Guerra-Bravo was transported to Denver Health Medical Center following the shooting and died there on Aug. 30.

According to the DA's office, officers had responded to a call of a man harassing a homeowner near East 50th Avenue and Washington Street. Body camera footage released in July shows officers approaching Guerra-Bravo, who walked away while carrying what both officers believed was a knife; after being ordered to stop, Guerra-Bravo ran and then rounded a corner where Egbert says the man lunged at him. Egbert fired six shots. The camera was partially obstructed at the moment of the alleged lunge, leaving the exact encounter unclear.

'After a thorough review of the evidence in the case, I believe that the use of force by Officer Egbert was justified based on Colorado law regarding use of force in self defense and in defense of others,' Walsh said in the release. The decision closes the criminal investigation into the shooting, though questions about transparency have been raised given the weeks-long delay in publicly disclosing Guerra-Bravo's cause of death.

stories.headline: Thunderstorms Delay More Than 400 Flights at Denver International Airport
stories.summary:
A Federal Aviation Administration ground delay issued Saturday afternoon caused widespread disruptions at Denver International Airport, with more than 477 flights delayed and 10 canceled as of 5:40 p.m. The FAA cited thunderstorms in the Denver area when it issued the delay around 4 p.m., with the restriction expected to last through 8 p.m.

United Airlines led all carriers with 175 delayed flights, followed by Southwest with 147 and SkyWest with 86. Cancellations were spread among Southwest, United, American and Envoy Air, with three flights each for the first two carriers and two each for the latter pair.

Severe storms sweeping across the Front Range and eastern plains Saturday brought the threat of ping-pong ball-sized hail and winds up to 60 mph to rural areas east of Denver, with the National Weather Service forecasting the greatest severe weather risk north of Pueblo between 3 and 9 p.m. Forecasters said Sunday would bring cooler, fall-like conditions with highs in the low 70s and a lower chance of storms.

stories.headline: Optiv Security Quietly Relocates Headquarters from Denver to Kansas
stories.summary:
Denver-based cybersecurity firm Optiv Security has relocated its corporate headquarters to Kansas, dealing a blow to Denver's technology sector. The move was made quietly, without a public announcement, and represents the departure of one of the region's more prominent tech employers from the local business community.

Optiv, which provides cybersecurity advisory and managed services to enterprise clients, had been headquartered in Denver for years and was considered a significant anchor in the city's growing tech industry. The relocation raises concerns about Denver's ability to retain established technology companies amid rising costs and competitive offers from other metros.

The departure adds to a broader set of economic pressures facing the Denver metro, including a state budget deficit driven by surging Medicaid costs and elevated diesel prices straining local businesses. City and state officials have not yet publicly responded to the relocation.

stories.headline: Littleton Approves 30-Year Tax Incentive to Land Scheels Sporting Goods Flagship Store
stories.summary:
Littleton city officials have approved a 30-year tax incentive package to attract a Scheels sporting goods flagship store to the area, marking a significant retail development deal for the south metro Denver suburb. Scheels, a privately held sporting goods retailer known for large-format experiential stores that often include Ferris wheels and aquariums, operates flagship locations in several western states.

The length and scale of the incentive reflect the competition among Colorado communities to land major retail anchors, particularly as traditional retail struggles in some markets. City leaders indicated the store is expected to generate significant sales tax revenue and create jobs once operational.

Details of the total incentive value and the precise location of the proposed store were not immediately available. Scheels flagships typically draw customers from broad regional trade areas, potentially boosting surrounding retail and restaurant businesses in Littleton.

stories.headline: Moose Attacks Hiker Near Boulder, Leaves Hoof-Print Bruise on Victim's Back
stories.summary:
A man was attacked by a mother moose while hiking in the mountains near Boulder, surviving with cuts, bruises and a hoof-print-shaped mark on his back. The group — a visiting couple and their son, who lives in Louisville — encountered a baby moose near a waterfall on a switchback trail during their descent, and the mother moose charged before the group could retreat.

The man threw his trekking pole as the moose charged and fell during the encounter, after which the animal stepped on his back. Another hiker began throwing rocks, prompting the moose to flee. A physician assistant who witnessed the incident from nearby provided first aid from her kit so the group could complete the two-mile hike out and seek emergency care.

The incident is a reminder of the dangers of encountering moose, particularly mothers with calves, in Colorado's mountain terrain. Colorado Parks and Wildlife advises hikers to give moose a wide berth and to use trees or other large objects as barriers if charged.

stories.headline: Interactive Tool Lets Colorado Voters Weigh State Budget Tradeoffs Ahead of Fall Ballot
stories.summary:
A new interactive tool called Colorado Tradeoffs, developed by the University of Colorado School of Public Affairs, Weigh In and COLab, allows residents to explore how this fall's major ballot measures could affect the state budget. The tool, available in English and Spanish and accessible on phones and desktops, guides users through the fiscal tradeoffs involved in the graduated income tax and TABOR measures appearing on November ballots.

Users can see how their choices compare with other Coloradans through a public dashboard, and participants are invited to join statewide online deliberations on Oct. 10 and 13. The tool is part of a broader election toolkit being tested by Colorado media organizations, alongside a 'Your Share' feature showing how individual tax dollars are allocated and a 'Build Your Own Ballot' tool personalized by address.

'It's a simple, interactive way for people to explore how the graduated income tax and TABOR ballot measures could affect Colorado's budget — and the tradeoffs that follow,' said COLab executive director Laura Frank. The resource arrives as voters prepare to weigh measures with significant implications for the state's ability to address its projected $1.6 billion budget shortfall.

topStory.headline: Ukraine Launches Largest-Ever Drone Attack on Moscow Region, Killing Two and Striking Major Oil Refinery
topStory.summary:
Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight Saturday into Sunday, with approximately 450 of them targeting the Moscow region in what officials on both sides described as the largest such assault on the Russian capital since the war began. The attack killed two people in the Moscow region — a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman — and wounded at least 20 others, according to Moscow regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov. A drone also struck a 21-story residential building, forcing the evacuation of roughly 400 residents, and a fire broke out at the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukrainian military officials said supplies more than a third of the region's fuel.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin confirmed the refinery and a residential building near one of the capital's boulevards were hit, and said temporary flight restrictions were imposed at Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo airports, both of which halted arrivals and departures overnight before lifting restrictions by Sunday morning. Sobyanin characterized the strike as 'an attempt to disrupt' Russia's three-day parliamentary elections, which concluded Sunday. Russian state media also reported that a drone attack on a civilian bus in a Moscow-controlled area of Kherson region killed two people, including an election official, citing the head of Russia's Central Election Commission.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly praised the strikes, writing on social media that Kyiv had deployed a combination of drones and domestically produced missiles — including the Flamingo and Pelican — to strike Russian oil and logistics infrastructure. 'These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine,' Zelenskyy wrote, framing the campaign as economic as well as military pressure on Moscow. Ukraine's defence minister said attacking fuel facilities 'directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression.'

The assault came as Russia simultaneously intensified its own strikes on Ukraine. A Russian attack on Fastiv in the Kyiv region on Saturday killed a mother and her two young children, and a separately injured child later died in hospital, according to regional officials. In the northeastern Sumy region, additional casualties were reported, and Zelenskyy said a Russian drone struck a monastery in the Kherson region, killing a member of the clergy and wounding four others.

The exchange underscores a sharp escalation in long-range strikes by both sides, with Ukraine increasingly targeting Russian energy infrastructure as a strategy to strain Kremlin finances and military logistics. The attack coincided with the final day of Russia's parliamentary elections, which are held in part across four Ukrainian regions Moscow illegally annexed and do not fully control. In a related development, the U.S. State Department approved a potential $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine last week, and President Donald Trump signed legislation introducing new sanctions designed to pressure Russia over the conflict.
